# Week 4 report: serving layer, integration tests, load test

*Generated by `loadtest/render_report.py` from `docs/loadtest_results_*.json`. Re-run the benchmark on your own
hardware and regenerate; the absolute numbers below belong to the machine described in section 3.*

## 1. Summary

* The champion XGBoost model is served by a FastAPI app (`serving/`) that reuses the Week-3 `data_pipeline.py` and
  pickled preprocessor unchanged.
* **36 integration tests pass.** The key one scores the 200 held-out test rows over HTTP and reproduces the training-time
  test Gini (0.8169) to 4 decimals. Three deliberately injected bugs were each caught by the suite (section 2).
* **50 concurrent requests: 0 errors in 26,985 requests** across every configuration and both load clients.
* With 50 requests in flight on a **single shared vCPU**, the default configuration sustained
  **366 req/s** with a median latency of **126 ms** and p95 of
  **228 ms** (lean client). A single request on an idle server takes **2 ms** (p50).
* The service needs about **2.6 ms of CPU per request**, i.e. an estimated
  **~389 req/s per core** (upper bound; see caveats).

## 2. Integration tests (`tests/test_integration.py`, `pytest -v`)

| Area | What is asserted |
|---|---|
| Contract | Response fields, probability in [0,1], `score = 300 + 600(1-p)`, band consistent with thresholds, SHAP factors have the right sign and order |
| Validation | 14 bad payloads (out-of-range, wrong type, unknown category, unknown field, null) and 5 missing-field cases all return **422**; malformed JSON 422; 404/405 |
| Faithfulness | **HTTP scoring of the 200 test rows gives the Gini stored in `champion_model_metadata.json` (0.8169, tolerance 1e-4) and exceeds the 0.45 target**; bands are monotone (low < medium < high default rate) |
| No train/serve skew | Fast path == Week-3 pipeline path to 1e-9 on **all 1,000 rows**, including the factors shown; served probabilities == offline `predict_proba` |
| Explanations | SHAP is additive (contributions sum to the margin); probability and SHAP use the same 16 trees (not the 46 stored); guard test fails if all 46 are used |
| Waterfall / UI | SHAP waterfall steps chain start-to-end and finish exactly at the predicted score; the built React UI is served from the same origin without shadowing API routes |
| Batch | Batch result equals 25 single calls; empty and >500 batches rejected |
| Concurrency (real 2-process uvicorn) | 100 requests with 50 in flight: all 200 OK, results identical to sequential scoring; a 50/50 mix of good and bad requests: every good one 200, every bad one 422 |

**Do the tests have teeth?** Three bugs were injected into a copy of the code: a wrong credit-score bin edge, using all 46
trees instead of 16, and skipping the scaler. The suite failed on each (1, 3 and 5+ failing tests respectively), including
the end-to-end Gini test for the last two.

## 3. Load-test method

* **Hardware:** Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.80GHz, **1 logical CPU(s)**, Linux-6.18.44-fc-v236-x86_64-with-glibc2.39. The load generator runs on the *same* machine as the server.
* **Software:** Python 3.12.3, xgboost 3.4.1, scikit-learn 1.9.1, pandas 3.0.6, FastAPI 0.162.0, uvicorn 0.54.0.
* **Traffic:** `POST /predict` (with SHAP explanation) using random real rows from the dataset, fixed seed, keep-alive connections, localhost.
* **Scenarios:** *burst* = 50 requests fired at the same instant, 20 rounds; *sustained* = 50 virtual users looping with no think time for
  20 s; *ramp* = 1/10/25/50/100 users for 8 s each.
* **Two load clients**, because a heavy client can starve the server on a small machine: `httpx` (a realistic Python client, ~4.4 ms CPU/request) and a
  **lean raw-socket client** (~0.1 ms CPU/request) that leaves nearly all the CPU to the server. The lean client is the better
  measure of the *server*; the httpx client is closer to what a Python caller would see.
* **Configurations:** *reference pipeline* = every request runs the Week-3 pandas `engineer_features` + `transform`;
  *fast path* = NumPy re-implementation, proven identical by test.
* Latency is measured by the client from send to full response. "Server-side" is the `X-Process-Time-Ms` header: time inside the app
  (excludes time spent waiting in the socket/accept queue).

## 5. Interpretation

1. **The fast path is 8.0x the throughput of the reference pipeline** under 50 concurrent users
   (366 vs 46 req/s). The pandas path costs about
   23 ms of CPU per request versus 3 ms. Both give bit-identical answers (tested), so the reference
   path is kept as a switch (`FINWISE_SCORING_PATH=pipeline`), not removed.
2. **Latency at 50 concurrent users is queueing, not slow scoring.** One request on an idle server takes ~2 ms
   and costs 2.6 ms of CPU. With 50 in flight on one core, Little's law gives 50 users / 366 req/s ≈ 137 ms
   average residence time, which matches the measured mean. The server-side header (p50 100 ms) is close to the
   client figure because it starts when the app receives the request, so it includes waiting for a thread and a turn on the CPU; it is not pure compute.
   The httpx numbers differ because the Python client itself used most of the core (section 4.4): its server-side p50 was only 18 ms
   while the client saw 257 ms, so those figures mostly measure the load generator.
3. **Saturation point.** On this 1-vCPU machine throughput stops growing at roughly 10 users; beyond that, extra users only add latency.
4. **Two workers did not help here, and that is expected.** The machine has 1 core, so a second process just competes
   for it. Rule of thumb: `--workers` = number of cores. On N cores, expect roughly N times the single-core figure until the CPU is saturated (not measured here).
5. **A run-to-run spread of about ±20% is normal on this shared sandbox** (the same fast-path/50-user httpx configuration measured
   130 req/s in this run and 151 / 163 req/s in earlier trial runs). Quote ranges, not single numbers.
6. **Tried and rejected:** running `/predict` inline on the event loop (`async def`) instead of the threadpool. Measured
   163 vs ~150 req/s, within noise, so it was reverted: the threadpool version keeps `/health` responsive under load.

## 6. Caveats (read before quoting these numbers)

* One shared vCPU, load generator on the same host, loopback network: absolute numbers will differ on real infrastructure.
  The *ratios* (fast vs reference, saturation shape) and the CPU-per-request figures transfer better than absolute req/s.
* The capacity estimate (~389 req/s/core) ignores real NIC/kernel/TLS/proxy overhead and is an upper bound.
* Every request includes a SHAP explanation and waterfall. `explain=False` would be faster; not exposed by the API.
* Test duration is seconds to minutes, not a multi-hour soak: memory growth and tail behaviour over time are untested.
* Tested here with newer library versions (xgboost 3.4.1, scikit-learn 1.9.1) than training (3.2.0 / 1.3.0). The pins in
  `requirements-serving.txt` match training but were **not** installed in this sandbox; run `pytest` in your pinned environment, since the parity tests will catch any skew.
* The dataset is small and appears synthetic; model-quality conclusions do not carry over to production data.
* The model's probability is uncalibrated (class-weighted training); use the risk band for decisions.

## 7. Reproduce

```bash
pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
pytest -v
python loadtest/loadtest.py --client httpx
python loadtest/loadtest.py --client lean
python loadtest/render_report.py
```
